newsitem.title: INDIA: India says foreign debt falls, but caution needed.
newsitem.headline: India says foreign debt falls, but caution needed.

text.p: India said on Thursday there was a significant fall in its external debt but added it needed to do more to reduce its indebtedness which continued to be a matter of concern.

The stock of external debt declined to $92.20 billion at the end of 1995/96 (April-March) from $99.01 billion one year earlier, the government said in a status report on external debt presented to parliament.
"There has been a substantial improvement in the external debt indicators in the last few years," the report said.
"This indicates that the strategy of export promotion and capping expensive borrowings has been successful in containing the burden of debt," it added.
But the report sounded a note of caution.

"The achievements however should not lead to complacency. The size of debt is still high by international standards, and debt service payments continue to make sizeable claim on our foreign exchange earnings," it said.

The government said in a statement summarising the report that India's debt-service ratio -- interest and principal payments as a percentage of exports -- fell to 25.54 at the end of March 1996 from 27.55 one year earlier.
It was as high as 35.25 in 1990-91, when a foreign exchange crunch forced India to launch a radical free-market reform programme to transform the economy.

The statement said the improvements were welcome but the emphasis now had to be on "consolidating existing gains and bringing debt to more manageable levels through sustaining the momentum of export growth, effective management of the existing debt and careful planning of future borrowings".

India said it ranked fourth behind Brazil, Mexico and China among the world's top debtors in overall terms but ranked itself sixth after these four nations and Indonesia and Russia in terms of present value (PV) of debt that discounted instalments of future principal and interest payments.

About three quarters of the decline in debt stock between end-March 1995 and end-March 1996 was attributable to the appreciation of the U.S. dollar against major international currencies, the statement said.

"However, as much as $1.69 billion out of the total decline of $6.81 billion is real -- the decline would have taken place even if the cross rates between U.S dollar and other currencies had remained unchanged," the statement added.

Concessional debt has remained steady at about 45 percent of total external debt, while the ratio of short-term debt to total debt, which touched 10.2 percent at the end of March 1991, fell to 5.5 percent by the end of March 1996, it said.
"India is relatively well-placed with respect to short-term debt," the report said.
"The stress has to be on consolidating the existing gains and to bring debt to more manageable levels," the report said.

"The debt management exercise should focus on changing the currency, maturity and interest mix of debt to reduce the cost of borrowings, minimising currency and interest risk and avoiding bunching of repayments," it said.
